edges.effect_quant: Occupational meta-analyses consistently place repetitive or awkward hand-wrist work on the harmful side of carpal-tunnel risk.
edges.population: workers with repetitive or constrained hand-wrist tasks
edges.mechanism: Repetitive forceful hand use and sustained wrist deviation can raise pressure within the carpal tunnel and promote cumulative median-nerve irritation. The mechanical pathway is direct enough that this edge reads more like classic occupational ergonomics than speculative epidemiology.
edges.summary: The best synthesis found that non-neutral wrist posture and repetitive occupational hand demands were associated with higher odds of carpal tunnel syndrome in workers. Earlier meta-analytic and occupational-disease reviews reported the same general direction, which makes this one of the cleaner repetitive-strain relationships in the batch.
edges.caveats: Exposure definitions range from self-reported repetition to measured posture and force, so effect estimates are not identical across studies. Non-work contributors such as obesity, diabetes, and anatomy still shape absolute risk.

evidence.citation: You D et al 2014 Saf Health Work
evidence.notes: Meta-analysis: association between wrist posture and carpal tunnel syndrome among workers.
